introduction-why-excel-fails-in-the-clou.core: Static spreadsheet forecasts assume fixed usage, but cloud spend varies with traffic, autoscaling, launches and price changes. You need models that capture trends, seasonality and uncertainty ranges.

first_principles.problem: A single-number forecast is off by 30%, and finance loses trust in engineering's numbers.
truths: Ranges are more honest than single points.

analogy.title: Forecasting a restaurant's food costs vs. a beach café's
analogy.story: A restaurant with bookings is predictable; a beach café depends on weather, tourists and events, so you plan for ranges.
analogy.breaks: Fancy models don't fix bad input data, so clean the history first.

check.q: Why do single-number cloud forecasts fail?
check.a: Cloud spend depends on many uncertain, elastic drivers that a fixed estimate can't capture.

monte-carlo-simulations-for-cloud-spend.core: Monte Carlo defines a probability distribution for each uncertain driver (traffic growth, cost per request, launch timing), samples them thousands of times, and produces a distribution of possible spend (P10/P50/P90).

first_principles.problem: With several uncertain variables, best-case and worst-case guesses are useless extremes.
truths: Each driver has a plausible range.

analogy.title: Weather forecasting ensembles
analogy.story: Meteorologists run many slightly varied simulations to say 'a 70% chance of rain'.
analogy.breaks: Garbage distributions give garbage output, so base the ranges on history.

code.text:
import numpy as np
N = 10_000
growth = np.random.normal(1.25, 0.08, N)     # yearly traffic
cpr = np.random.triangular(0.8, 1.0, 1.3, N) # $ per 1k req multiplier
spend = 2.4e6 * growth * cpr
print(np.percentile(spend, [10, 50, 90]))

check.q: What does a P90 forecast mean?
check.a: There's a 90% probability that spend will be at or below that value.

time-series-forecasting-the-foundation-b.core: Historical spend and usage reveal trend, weekly and yearly seasonality and events. Decompose them (Prophet, ARIMA) to forecast the baseline and to set realistic ranges for Monte Carlo inputs.

first_principles.problem: Simulation ranges are guessed, ignoring clear patterns like Black Friday spikes and weekend dips.
derivation: Use the **residual spread** to size the uncertainty.

analogy.title: Tide tables
analogy.story: Tides follow predictable cycles; you forecast them from history, then add a margin for storms.
analogy.breaks: Structural changes (re-architecture, new pricing) break historical patterns.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A baseline with intervals that captures the Black Friday spike.

code.text:
from prophet import Prophet
m = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=True, weekly_seasonality=True)
m.add_country_holidays("US")
m.fit(df.rename(columns={"date": "ds", "cost": "y"}))
fc = m.predict(m.make_future_dataframe(90))

check.q: Why do time-series forecasting before Monte Carlo?
check.a: History provides realistic baselines and variance ranges for the simulation's inputs.

auto-scaling-and-budget-variance.core: In the cloud, spend variance often means success: autoscaling served more demand. Judge variance against business drivers (cost per unit) rather than against a fixed budget alone, and set flexible, driver-based budgets.

first_principles.problem: Finance flags a 20% overspend as a failure when traffic grew 30% and unit cost fell.
truths: Unit cost separates efficiency from volume.
derivation: Use **flexible budgets** (budget = units × target unit cost).

analogy.title: A taxi company's fuel budget
analogy.story: Fuel spend above budget is good news if rides grew more than fuel did.
analogy.breaks: Unbounded autoscaling can also mean runaway bugs, so keep anomaly detection running.

example.title: Variance decomposition

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The conversation shifts from blame to insight.

example.outcome: budgets match how the cloud behaves.

check.q: What is a flexible budget in cloud FinOps?
check.a: A budget that scales with business volume, such as units multiplied by a target unit cost.

cogs-reduction-programs.core: For a growing company the goal isn't a smaller bill but lower COGS per unit of revenue. Run structured programmes with unit-cost targets, prioritised initiatives (architecture, commitments, waste) and tracked margin impact.

first_principles.problem: 'Cut the cloud bill' mandates conflict with 50% growth, frustrate engineers and miss the real goal: margin.
truths: Initiatives need prioritising by impact and effort.
derivation: Set a **target**, e.g. COGS from 18% to 14% of revenue.
Build an **initiative backlog** (rightsizing, Graviton, storage tiering, commitments).

analogy.title: A factory reducing cost per widget
analogy.story: Output keeps growing, but each widget gets cheaper through process improvements.
analogy.breaks: Over-optimising can hurt reliability or velocity, so balance against SLOs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Margin up 4 points while revenue grew 50%.

check.q: Why target COGS as a % of revenue instead of the absolute bill?
check.a: In a growing company spend rises with usage, and what matters is efficiency and margin.
